name: Skin whitening/bleaching

angle.text: Users apply or take lightening agents to fade dark spots and lift overall skin tone, and some forum posters say it raises their rating by about 0.5 to 1 PSL. Topical agents such as hydroquinone and arbutin have clinical study for pigmentation; the rating claim rests on anecdote.

summary: Lightening skin tone with topical agents, supplements or injections, discussed in looksmaxxing circles as a way to raise appearance scores; the practice is long-established worldwide and carries well-documented risks.
note: Regulators and reviews document harms from mercury, steroid and hydroquinone products and from intravenous glutathione.
currentQuick:
Skin whitening means using chemical agents to reduce melanin and lighten skin tone. It predates the internet by centuries and is practiced in many regions for cultural, social and medical reasons. On looksmaxxing forums it appears as a method some posters say improves their ratings.
Research exists on individual agents such as kojic acid, hydroquinone and glutathione, mostly in the context of pigmentation disorders. Dermatology reviews also describe cosmetic lightening as a public health and sociocultural issue.
How it works: Most lightening agents work by inhibiting tyrosinase, the key enzyme in melanin production. Others block the transfer of melanin to skin cells or destroy melanocytes. Glutathione is reported to inhibit tyrosinase and shift melanin production from eumelanin toward phaeomelanin.
Risks and caveats: Reported harms include mercury toxicity from contaminated products, skin thinning and other effects from long-term steroid creams, ochronosis and contact dermatitis from hydroquinone, and serious reactions from intravenous glutathione. Many products are restricted or banned in several countries, and sun sensitivity rises in users.
deepLead:
Skin whitening, also called skin lightening or bleaching, is the use of chemical substances to lighten skin color or even out tone by reducing melanin. Recorded practices date back more than two thousand years, and use is widespread across Africa, Asia and elsewhere. 
A 2022 dermatology review describes cosmetic skin lightening as a growing public health problem among communities of color, with well-documented adverse health effects alongside social and cultural drivers.  Reviews of the agents themselves, such as glutathione, describe a gap between popular use and evidence of efficacy and safety. 
On looksmax.org the topic is discussed by some users as a looksmaxxing tactic, often alongside ethnicity and the PSL rating scale; posts include claims that lightening adds to a rating and recommendations of particular products.

name: Pheromone cologne

angle.text: Buyers wear these scents hoping the added pheromones make them more attractive to others, as a fragrance-based add-on to grooming and presentation. The attraction effect is based on marketing and anecdote, and reviewers report no human pheromone shown to change behavior.

summary: Scents sold with the claim that added pheromones make the wearer more attractive; reviewers say no human pheromone has been shown to change behavior.
note: Marketing claims of sexual attraction are described by reviewers as unsupported by peer-reviewed evidence.
currentQuick:
Pheromone colognes are fragrances or sprays sold with the claim that they contain human sex pheromones that increase attraction. The concept draws on research into compounds such as androstenone and androstadienone.
A widely cited encyclopedia summary says no pheromonal substance has been shown in a peer-reviewed study to directly influence human behavior, and describes the area as speculative and controversial.
How it works: Proposed mechanisms involve steroid compounds from sweat glands acting through the vomeronasal organ or olfactory receptors. The human vomeronasal organ is described as atrophied or absent in adults with nonfunctional receptor genes, and whether it detects pheromones is disputed.
Risks and caveats: Reported direct risks are those of any fragrance product, such as skin irritation or allergy in some users. The main caveat reviewers raise is that effects on attraction are not demonstrated.
deepLead:
Pheromone cologne is a perfume or body spray marketed with the claim that it contains human pheromones that make the wearer more sexually attractive. Wikipedia reports that such claims are unsupported by peer-reviewed evidence. 
The scientific literature on human pheromones centers on axillary steroids such as androstenol, androstenone and androstadienone, with some small studies reporting effects on mood or attention. Wikipedia notes the field has been criticized for small samples, publication bias and weak methods, and describes the role of human pheromones as speculative and controversial. 
In looksmaxxing circles, scent is sometimes discussed as one more component of appearance and presentation, and Wikipedia's article on looksmaxxing mentions offshoots such as smellmaxxing.

name: Frenotomy / tongue tie release for face

angle.text: Forum posters discuss releasing the tongue frenulum so the tongue can rest against the palate, in the hope of a more defined jaw, better profile and straighter teeth. Studies cover feeding and speech outcomes; the facial-appearance link is untested and rests on anecdote.

summary: Surgical release of the tongue's frenulum, discussed online as a step toward better tongue posture and jaw development; studies cover feeding and speech, not facial appearance.
note: Evidence for facial or jaw changes from tongue-tie release is absent; documented benefits are studied for infant feeding and some speech outcomes, and rare major complications are reported.
currentQuick:
Tongue-tie (ankyloglossia) is a condition in which the band of tissue under the tongue limits its movement. Releasing it is a short procedure called a frenotomy or frenectomy. Some online discussions of jaw and face development link tongue posture and tongue-tie release to appearance.
Published research examines breastfeeding, speech and sleep outcomes. No study found tests the procedure for changing facial structure in adults or children.
How it works: The procedure cuts or reshapes the lingual frenulum, sometimes with a laser, to increase tongue mobility. Proponents of the facial link argue that a freer tongue can rest against the palate; Wikipedia notes this posture is associated with nasal breathing and that associations with palate and jaw development are presented as hypotheses.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe the procedure as simple with low complication rates in infants, but case reports and a systematic review document major complications after tongue-tie release. Experts disagree about how often tongue-tie causes problems and about diagnosis, particularly of posterior tongue-tie.
deepLead:
Frenotomy, also called frenectomy or frenuloplasty, is the surgical release of the lingual frenulum in people with tongue-tie (ankyloglossia). It is established for some infants with breastfeeding difficulty, and its use for speech, sleep and other outcomes is debated. 
Appearance-focused communities discuss tongue-tie release as part of a story about tongue posture and jaw development. No published human study has tested frenotomy as a way of changing facial structure. 
Systematic reviews report mixed evidence on speech outcomes, and a scoping review of non-infants found improvements in tongue movement with treatment, while noting that definitions and diagnostic criteria for tongue-tie are not generally agreed.

name: Face rating apps / AI scoring

angle.text: Users submit photos to apps and AI tools to get an attractiveness number or tier, then track it across haircuts, grooming changes or angles, and some convert it to PSL. The scores are model outputs, and accuracy as a guide to real-world appeal is largely unstudied.

summary: Apps and AI tools that score a face photo for attractiveness, popular in looksmaxxing; the scores are model outputs, and a notable early contest drew bias complaints.
note: Scores are not validated measures; a 2016 AI beauty contest was criticized for racially skewed results.
currentQuick:
Face rating apps use algorithms to give a photo a numeric attractiveness score, often on scales borrowed from looksmaxxing such as PSL. They are used to track self-improvement or to compare faces.
The sources available describe the category only in general terms, and no validation study of these specific apps was found. A well-known early example, the Beauty.AI contest, generated controversy over biased results.
How it works: Such tools typically assess features such as facial symmetry, blemishes, wrinkles and estimated age, and sometimes resemblance to reference faces, as Beauty.AI did. Research on symmetry shows it raises attractiveness ratings, but also that findings are modest and nuanced.
Risks and caveats: Reported concerns include bias from training data and the effect on self-image of numeric scoring; Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article describes commentators linking the wider culture to body dysmorphia. Scores differ between apps and are not validated clinical measures.
deepLead:
Face rating apps and AI scoring tools estimate a person's attractiveness from a photograph and return a number or tier. In looksmaxxing they are used alongside forum ratings and paid analyses by content creators, and some report results on community scales such as PSL. 
A reference point from outside the community is Beauty.AI, a 2016 app-based contest by Youth Laboratories in which artificial intelligence judged symmetry, blemishes, wrinkles, estimated age and resemblance to models among more than 60,000 entrants. Of 44 winners, 37 were white, which critics cited as evidence of bias; the company attributed it partly to limited data.

name: PSL scale

angle.text: Community members use the PSL scale as a shared yardstick to rate male faces and to measure progress from changes such as skin, hair or leanness. It is an informal forum system, not scientifically validated, and ratings reflect community opinion.

summary: The community rating system, roughly 1 to 8, for male facial attractiveness; it is informal and not scientifically validated.
note: An unvalidated, subjective scale; critics link the surrounding culture to distress and body-image concerns.
currentQuick:
PSL stands for Perceived Sexual Levels, an informal scale used in looksmaxxing communities to rate facial attractiveness, usually from 1 to 8. Its name is said to combine three forum sites on which it arose.
It sets out tiers from below average through 'normie' and 'Chadlite' up to 'Chad' and beyond. Sources describe it as subjective and not scientifically validated.
How it works: Raters judge faces on features that community explanations group under harmony, dimorphism, angularity and individual features. Because individual raters differ, scores vary; forum users also debate whether PSL differs from what they call 'appeal', a broader notion of attractiveness.
Risks and caveats: The scale itself carries no physical risk. Commentators cited by Wikipedia criticize the surrounding culture for tiering people and link it to body dysmorphia and distress; the Wikipedia article also carries a neutrality-dispute tag.
deepLead:
The PSL scale, short for Perceived Sexual Levels, is an informal system for rating male facial attractiveness on roughly a 1 to 8 range. Wikipedia reports it was created on three forums, PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, whose initials form the acronym; the forums are defunct but the terminology spread to wider social media. 
Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, describes the scale as based on harmony, dimorphism, angularity and individual features, and as not scientifically validated.  No published study has evaluated the scale itself.

name: Canthal tilt theory

chain: Eyes read as sharper, more alert
angle.text: Forum users measure the angle of the eye corners and treat a positive tilt as a marker of attractiveness, with some suggesting posture, mewing or surgery to change it. The tilt itself is measurable; the strong rule built on it and the non-surgical change claims are poorly studied.

summary: The idea that the upward or downward angle of the eye corners drives how attractive a face is; the angle is real and measurable, the strong rule built on it is not well studied.
note: Surgical and DIY 'fixes' discussed online carry the usual risks of eyelid and orbital procedures; no trial tests the attractiveness rule itself.
currentQuick:
Canthal tilt is the angle of the line joining the inner and outer corners of the eye relative to horizontal. In looksmaxxing communities a 'positive' tilt (outer corner higher than the inner) is treated as a mark of an attractive, masculine or 'predatory' look, while a 'negative' tilt (outer corner lower) is treated as a handicap.
Surgeons and anthropometry researchers measure canthal tilt as a routine photographic landmark, and average values have been reported for some groups. The stronger claim, that tilt is a primary driver of attractiveness, has little direct published testing, and forum threads mostly debate whether it can be changed.
How it works: Tilt is determined by the position of the eye corners (canthi), which are anchored by the lateral and medial canthal tendons and the shape of the bony orbit. Forum users argue that cheekbone and upper-jaw support changes it; surgeons describe procedures such as canthoplasty that alter the outer corner. Makeup and lash styling can change how tilt appears without altering anatomy.
Risks and caveats: Measuring tilt carries no risk. Procedures people discuss to change it (canthopexy or canthoplasty, filler, orbital or midface surgery) are medical procedures with the ordinary surgical risks, and some forum threads describe do-it-yourself approaches that clinicians would not endorse. Community discussion also links the concept with distress for some users who describe a negative tilt as decisive.
deepLead:
Canthal tilt is the angle between a horizontal line and the line joining the inner corner (medial canthus) and outer corner (lateral canthus) of the eye. In looksmaxxing slang a positive tilt means the outer corner sits higher than the inner corner, a neutral tilt means they are level, and a negative tilt means the outer corner sits lower.
The canthal tilt theory is the community belief that this angle is a major determinant of facial attractiveness, especially in men, and that a positive tilt signals a dominant or masculine look, often paired with the term 'hunter eyes'. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists canthal tilt among the core terms of the subculture.
Outside the community, canthal tilt appears as a measurement in plastic surgery and craniofacial research, for example in studies of eyelid surgery, facial feminization surgery and congenital skull-shape correction. Studies of beauty-pageant winners and of attractiveness have reported tilt values or examined it as a cue, but no large trial has established it as a principal driver of attractiveness.

name: Hunter eyes

angle.text: Hunter eyes are described online as an ideal eye area, with a positive tilt, deep set and low brows, and some users try squinting or exercises to approximate it. There is no formal medical definition and little direct research on attractiveness or on trainability.

summary: A looksmaxxing label for deep-set, slightly hooded eyes with an upward tilt; popular as an ideal online, with no formal medical definition and little direct research.
note: Not a recognized clinical category; surgeries sometimes discussed for it are ordinary eyelid and orbital procedures with their own risks.
currentQuick:
'Hunter eyes' is slang for an eye area described as narrow, deep-set and slightly hooded, with a positive canthal tilt, little visible white below the iris and low-set brows. It is contrasted with so-called 'prey eyes' that are rounder, show more white and tilt downward.
The term comes from looksmaxxing and related forums, where it is described as intimidating and attractive by some and as overrated or a 'meme' by others. It is not a term used in ophthalmology or anthropology, and no study has tested it as a category.
How it works: Believers attribute the look to bone structure: orbit shape, brow ridge and cheekbone support, plus soft-tissue factors like lid hooding. Non-surgical methods people discuss include makeup and squinting; surgical options discussed include canthoplasty, upper blepharoplasty and orbital procedures. Forum users disagree on whether any exercise can change it.
Risks and caveats: The concept itself carries no direct risk. Surgical and filler procedures talked about for the look carry standard risks (asymmetry, dry eye, vision-related complications, revision surgery). Some critics link the trend to appearance anxiety, and threads show users distressed over perceived eye-shape flaws.
deepLead:
Hunter eyes is an informal looksmaxxing term for an eye area said to look intense and masculine. Descriptions generally include a positive canthal tilt, deep-set eyes, limited upper-eyelid exposure and low-set eyebrows. The opposite is called 'prey eyes', described as rounder and showing more sclera with a negative tilt.
Grokipedia states the term has no formal classification in medical, anthropological or ophthalmological literature, and that comparisons to predator and prey eyes come from animal research rather than human face studies. Wikipedia lists hunter eyes among the community's core terms.
Within looksmax.org there is a long-running split. Some users call hunter eyes a signature of appeal, others dispute the value of the concept or argue it is determined by bone structure that exercise cannot change.

name: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR)

angle.text: Forum users calculate fWHR from photos and treat a higher ratio as a sign of masculinity and attractiveness, then weigh beards, hairstyles or procedures against it. Research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression; the attractiveness use is largely untested.

summary: Cheekbone width divided by upper-face height; real research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression, and forums treat it as a masculinity and attractiveness score.
note: Studies of what it predicts are mixed and effect sizes are small; measurement is sensitive to camera distance and landmark choice.
currentQuick:
FWHR is the width of the face across the cheekbones divided by the height from the upper lip to the brow. Researchers have studied it since the late 2000s as a possible cue of aggression, dominance and trustworthiness, mostly in men.
Looksmaxxing communities turned it into a numeric score, with wider values often described as more masculine, and some users measure their own face from photos. Published meta-analyses report a very small sex difference and a small link with aggression, and later studies have questioned several of the findings.
How it works: The ratio is thought by some researchers to be shaped by puberty hormones and facial growth, though a study of adolescents found no association with testosterone levels. Another line of research proposes that observers over-attribute aggression to wide faces. Forum users discuss it as a fixed bony trait and ask whether anything can change it.
Risks and caveats: Measuring FWHR itself is harmless. Camera distance and lens changes the measured value, which users have noted. Discussion of cosmetic or hormonal ways to widen the face, including among minors, involves medical interventions whose evidence is limited; no study shows that treatments change FWHR.
deepLead:
Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR or fWHR) is the distance between the cheekbones (bizygomatic width) divided by the height of the upper face, typically measured between the upper lip and the brow. It is a size-independent measure and has been studied as a possible sexually dimorphic cue linked to dominance, threat and aggression.
A 2015 meta-analysis found the ratio was larger in men than in women, with a small effect size (d = 0.11). A separate 2015 meta-analysis reported a small but significant positive relationship between men's FWHR and aggression. Other work has found the link depends on factors such as income, and some studies have not replicated it.
In looksmaxxing, FWHR became a standard metric. Grokipedia says community sources treat values around 1.8 or above as ideal for masculinity, while noting these are informal standards, and that scientific studies connect higher FWHR with perceived dominance and threat and often lower attractiveness ratings.

name: Golden ratio face analysis

angle.text: Forum posters measure features such as eye spacing and mouth-to-nose width against phi (about 1.618) and other ideal ratios to decide what to change. Research has found little support for phi as a driver of attractiveness, and the precision of the scores is unvalidated.

summary: Judging a face by how closely its proportions match phi (about 1.618) or a set of ideal ratios; popular in forums, with research finding little support for phi as a driver of attractiveness.
note: Ratio targets circulating online are informal standards, not validated clinical criteria.
currentQuick:
Golden ratio face analysis compares measurements of a face, such as mouth-to-nose width or facial thirds, with ideal ratios, often phi (about 1.618). Looksmaxxing forums post such analyses of celebrities and members, producing lists of 'ideal' and 'off' ratios.
Phi has a long history in claims about beauty, but a study in Malaysian adults summarized on Wikipedia reported no significant association between the golden ratio and attractiveness, and critics note many claimed examples in art do not hold up. The ratio targets used in looksmaxxing are described as informal community standards.
How it works: Participants photograph a face from the front and side, mark landmarks, compute ratios and compare them with target values. The underlying theory is that proportions near mathematical ideals signal harmony and are perceived as beautiful.
Risks and caveats: The analysis itself is harmless. Reported downsides are psychological: critics link the practice and its numeric scoring of faces to appearance anxiety and body dysmorphia, and the ratio targets are not validated for surgical planning.
deepLead:
Golden ratio face analysis is the practice of measuring facial proportions and comparing them with ideal values, most famously the golden ratio phi, about 1.618. In looksmaxxing forums the analyses are posted as lists of ratios, for example mouth-to-nose width, eye spacing and midface proportions, with each labelled ideal or off.
Wikipedia's golden ratio article notes that many claims connecting phi to art and nature are disputed. Examples include the Mona Lisa and the Vitruvian Man, which the article says are not supported by Leonardo's own writings or measurements. The article on physical attractiveness describes the golden ratio as a perceived measure of beauty in ancient Greece and summarizes a study of 286 young adults in Malaysia that found no significant association between the golden ratio and attractiveness.
Grokipedia says the ratio targets used in looksmaxxing are informal community standards rather than validated medical or scientific criteria.

name: Mogging / AMOG

angle.text: Looksmaxxers use mogging as slang for outshining another man in a given setting, and it frames goals such as height, jaw or style improvements. It is a social concept based on anecdote, with no research of its own.

summary: Looksmaxxing slang for outshining another man in appearance, from 'AMOG'; a social concept with no research of its own.
note: A social-comparison term; community threads show it can feed appearance anxiety.
currentQuick:
To 'mog' someone is to outclass them in looks or in a specific trait, so that they appear less attractive by comparison. The word is generally said to derive from AMOG, an abbreviation for 'alpha male of the group'. Forums split it into types such as face, height, frame and voice mogging.
It is a concept from the subculture, not a scientific term. Posts describe real or imagined social encounters where one man 'mogs' another, and a school of thought holds that comparison effects like this matter for how a man is perceived at a given moment.
How it works: The concept assumes that attractiveness is judged relatively: standing next to a more attractive or taller man is said to lower how you are perceived. People using the term compare face, height, body frame or voice. No published study tests the term itself, although research on social comparison and contrast effects exists more broadly.
Risks and caveats: Using the word carries no direct physical risk. Critics cited in coverage of looksmaxxing link the surrounding culture with body dysmorphia and distress, and many posts frame ordinary encounters as contests.
deepLead:
Mogging is looksmaxxing slang for asserting dominance or superiority over another person on the basis of appearance, outshining them in looks or in a particular trait. The word is generally said to come from AMOG, short for 'alpha male of the group'.
On forums, mogging is divided into types, including facial mogging, height mogging, frame (body) mogging and voice mogging. Some threads treat it as the central point of the whole enterprise, while others argue it is overemphasised.
No studies found. The term is a subculture concept without published research that tests it directly.

name: Black pill ideology

angle.text: The black pill is a belief from incel communities that genetics and looks largely fix a man's outcomes, and looksmaxxing forums discuss it as the pessimistic counterpart to improvement-focused approaches. Researchers have studied it mainly for links to mental-health burden and misogynistic extremism, not for effects on appearance.

summary: The incel-originated belief that genetics and looks largely fix a man's romantic and social outcomes; studied by researchers mainly for its links to mental-health burden and misogynistic extremism.
note: Researchers report associations with depression, social isolation and, in some branches of the community, endorsement of violence; some looksmaxxers reject the idea as fatalistic.
currentQuick:
The black pill is a worldview from online incel forums holding that dating and social success are determined largely by physical traits such as height and facial structure, and that unattractive men cannot escape this hierarchy. The name plays on the red pill and blue pill from The Matrix.
In looksmaxxing spaces it is a contested idea. Some users treat it as a motivation to optimise appearance, others as a source of despair, and some argue it undermines the self-improvement the subculture claims to offer. Academic research studies it mostly as part of incel ideology and its mental-health and violence-related correlates.
How it works: The belief rests on claims about evolved mate preferences, hypergamy and selected dating-site statistics. Researchers describe forum members using technology and data to argue that attraction is biologically determined, and some psychologists have proposed frameworks linking such narratives to rejection sensitivity, grievance and identity fusion.
Risks and caveats: Research on incel communities reports high rates of depression, suicidality and social isolation among members, and a minority endorsement of violence against women. A 2022 survey cited by Wikipedia found most self-identified incels rejected violence. Anyone in distress can contact local crisis services.
deepLead:
The black pill is a belief system associated with online incel (involuntary celibate) communities. Wikipedia describes it as a more nihilistic offshoot of the red pill idea, holding that dating and society mainly benefit women and physically attractive men and that unattractive men cannot escape this hierarchy because success is set by genetics. The pill metaphor comes from The Matrix.
In looksmaxxing, Wikipedia says the practice was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s and by the mid-2020s was more commonly linked with black pill ideology; the black pill is defined there as the belief that women's attraction depends mainly on physical traits like height and facial features. Many looksmaxxers dispute that the idea implies giving up, and threads debate whether blackpill thinking helps or harms self-improvement.
Academics study the black pill within research on incels, misogynistic extremism and mental health. A 2021 qualitative analysis of 9,062 comments on an incel forum found that members argue emerging technologies reveal and compound gender practices that produce involuntary celibacy. A 2024 study found identity fusion with the incel ingroup predicted endorsement of violence against women.

name: Halo effect

angle.text: Looksmaxxers cite the halo effect as the reason appearance gains pay off beyond looks, shaping how competent, likable and trustworthy others perceive them. The effect is well documented in psychology; community claims about its size across school, work and dating vary.

summary: The bias where one good trait, usually looks, colors how everything else about you is judged; well documented in psychology, central to looksmaxxing talk.
note: Effect sizes vary by trait, target sex and setting, and the bias can reverse (horn effect).
currentQuick:
The halo effect is a documented cognitive bias in which a positive impression in one area, such as physical attractiveness, leads people to rate a person more favorably on unrelated traits like intelligence, trustworthiness or competence. The term goes back to psychologist Edward Thorndike's 1920 paper on ratings, and the attractiveness version was popularized by the 1972 'what is beautiful is good' study. [1][2]
In looksmaxxing communities it is one of the most commonly cited ideas. Members use it as evidence that appearance changes how people are treated in school, work, dating and online, and often refer to a 'looks halo' that attractive people are said to enjoy. [3][4]
How it works: Researchers describe it as a general-impression effect: people fill in ambiguous information about someone to match a salient first impression. Proposed models include a general impression model, a salient dimension model and an inadequate discrimination model. The opposite pattern, in which one negative trait taints other judgments, is called the horn effect. [1]
Risks and caveats: The halo effect is a perception bias rather than something a person does, so it has no side effects of its own. Reviewers note that its strength varies, that it can reverse (for example, attractive defendants were punished more harshly in a mock swindle case), and that some critics argue part of the correlation between traits is real rather than illusory. [1][2]
deepLead:
The halo effect is a cognitive bias in which an overall positive impression of a person, brand or product in one area shapes judgments in other, unrelated areas. The term is credited to the psychologist Edward Thorndike, who in 1920 reported that military officers' ratings of their soldiers on separate qualities were suspiciously correlated, as if a general impression were coloring each specific judgment. 
In the study of physical appearance the idea is usually called the attractiveness halo or the 'what is beautiful is good' stereotype. In a 1972 experiment by Dion, Berscheid and Walster, students who viewed photographs rated attractive people as more socially desirable and as likely to have happier marriages and more successful careers.  Later work has examined the effect in essay grading, mock jury decisions, voting, trust games and ratings of beauty-filtered photos. 
In looksmaxxing communities the halo effect is a core concept. Members cite it as the mechanism by which facial attractiveness, height or other traits are said to cause other people to grant a person extra credibility, leniency and status.  Researchers treat the underlying bias as well established, while emphasizing that effect sizes differ across traits, target sex, culture and context, and that the bias can reverse in some situations.

name: Sexual market value (SMV)

chain: Looks form part of overall desirability
Changes to face and body shift it
angle.text: Manosphere and looksmaxxing users treat SMV as a total desirability score and use it to prioritise changes such as skin, hair, fitness and style. It is a community term loosely related to academic mate value research, and the community's specific weightings are untested.

summary: A manosphere and looksmaxxing term for a person's overall desirability as a partner, roughly the community cousin of academic 'mate value' and 'sexual capital' ideas.
note: SMV itself is a community concept with no standard measure; related academic research covers attractiveness, mate preferences and 'sexual capital'.
currentQuick:
Sexual market value (SMV) is slang for how desirable someone is as a sexual or romantic partner, treated as a score or rank in a marketplace. It originated on pick-up artist forums and spread through manosphere and incel-adjacent communities, where people compare themselves using decile scales, the PSL scale or a 'looks, money, status' framework. [1]
In looksmaxxing spaces SMV is the goal that appearance improvements are said to raise. Academic researchers do not use the term, but they study related ideas such as 'sexual capital', 'erotic capital' (Catherine Hakim), the pay premium for attractiveness and the matching hypothesis. [1][2]
How it works: SMV is described as a combination of traits such as facial attractiveness, height, body, status and money that determines who a person can attract. Community members rank themselves and others on numeric scales. Scholars describe related concepts, for example Adam Green's argument that desirability depends on the particular 'sexual field' and its local preferences. [1]
Risks and caveats: No validated instrument measures SMV, and critics of related academic theories argue that they overstate individual ownership of attractiveness and overlook culture, class and race. Community discussion also includes race-based tier lists and comparisons that scholars studying sexual racism describe as reflecting bias in dating markets. [1]
deepLead:
Sexual market value, usually abbreviated SMV, is a term used mainly in manosphere, pick-up artist and looksmaxxing communities for a person's overall desirability as a sexual or romantic partner. It treats dating as a market in which individuals have a comparable value that determines the partners they can attract. 
The term is not an established concept in academic psychology. The closest scholarly ideas are 'sexual capital' or 'erotic capital', terms used by sociologists and economists for the social power or resources a person gains from sexual attractiveness, and mate-value and matching research in social psychology. 
On looksmax.org SMV appears in ratings, 'SMV battle' threads comparing celebrities, and debates about how race, height and facial features affect it.  Looksmaxxing frames its projects, from skincare to surgery, as ways to raise SMV.

name: Jestermaxxing

angle.text: Forum users describe leaning on humor and clowning to win social and romantic interest, as a complement to looks. Research exists on humor and attraction generally, but the term and its claims about less attractive men are based on anecdote.

Jestermaxxing is looksmaxxing-forum slang for relying on humor, joking and playing the clown to gain social standing or attract partners, often discussed as a way to offset a lower facial attractiveness rating. Members describe friends who 'pull' this way and others who say it backfires. [1][2]

Jestermaxxing is a slang term in looksmaxxing communities for using humor, clowning or entertaining behavior to gain social acceptance or romantic interest. The word combines 'jester' with the '-maxxing' suffix used for optimization practices in these communities. 
On looksmax.org the term is discussed mainly as a social strategy that some members say works for people of lower attractiveness and others call ineffective or inauthentic.  No dedicated research or media coverage of the term was found.
Academic work on humor in mate selection is a related but separate area. Summaries report that humor is often named as a valued trait in partners, that its effect depends on context and on the humor's style, and that results differ across cultures.

name: Looksmatching

angle.text: Forum users use looksmatching to describe couples rated at a similar attractiveness level and to calibrate who they can expect to attract after improving. It parallels the psychology matching hypothesis, which has real but mixed support.

summary: Forum term for couples paired at a similar attractiveness level, the community version of the psychology 'matching hypothesis', which has real but mixed support.
note: Research supports similarity in partners' attractiveness on average, but effects are modest and measurement is noisy.
currentQuick:
Looksmatching is looksmaxxing slang for couples in which both partners are about equally attractive. It lines up with the matching hypothesis from social psychology, first proposed by Elaine Hatfield (then Walster) and colleagues in 1966, which holds that people tend to end up with partners of similar social desirability. [1]
In the community, the term is used descriptively, for example when a poster notes that most couples at a gathering were 'looksmatches'. [2] Research on the hypothesis finds support in couples and online dating data, alongside criticism of its methods and explanations. [1]
How it works: The matching hypothesis proposes that people aim for partners they can realistically attract, which sorts them into pairs of similar attractiveness. Critics argue the effect may reflect fear of rejection, proximity or shared status rather than a preference for similarity. [1]
Risks and caveats: No clinical risks apply. Reviewers note that attractiveness ratings are noisy and that research mostly uses student samples, so effect sizes are uncertain. [1]
deepLead:
Looksmatching is a term in looksmaxxing communities for couples whose members are rated as similarly attractive. Forum posts use it informally, for instance to remark that most of a group's couples were looksmatched. 
Academic psychology studies the same pattern as the matching hypothesis, proposed by Elaine Hatfield (Walster) and colleagues in 1966, which states that people tend to form committed relationships with partners of comparable social desirability, usually physical attractiveness. 
Little community material about the term exists beyond a single forum thread; this article therefore relies mainly on the research summary.

name: Norwood scale

chain: Fuller-looking hair or a planned cut
angle.text: Users place their hairline on the seven-stage Norwood chart to size up male pattern hair loss and choose among treatments, transplants, hair systems or a buzz cut. The scale is a standard clinical classification used by dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons.

summary: The standard seven-stage chart for grading male pattern hair loss, used by clinicians and constantly by forums to size up a hairline and plan treatment.
note: Visual and subjective: inter-rater agreement is described as variable, and it was built mainly on white men.
currentQuick:
The Norwood scale (Hamilton-Norwood scale) grades male pattern hair loss in seven stages, from a full head of hair (stage 1) to only a narrow band of hair around the sides and back (stage 7). It builds on a 1951 system by James B. Hamilton and a 1975 revision by dermatologist O'Tar Norwood. [1][2]
In looksmaxxing communities members use it to rate their own hairlines, decide when to start treatments, and judge how much hair loss affects attractiveness. Clinicians and trial investigators use it to stage patients and track treatment response. [1][3][4]
How it works: The scale is a visual classification, not a test. It describes how the hairline recedes at the temples and how thinning appears at the crown (vertex) as androgenetic alopecia progresses; 'A' variants describe frontal recession without a separate crown patch. [1][2]
Risks and caveats: The scale itself carries no risk. Reviewers report variable agreement between raters, limited fit for non-white populations, no information on how fast loss will progress, and a risk of self-misstaging, for example when judging wet hair. [2][5]
deepLead:
The Hamilton-Norwood scale, commonly called the Norwood scale, is a classification of male pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia) in seven main stages. It is widely used by dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons to describe severity, plan treatment and monitor change over time. 
The system goes back to James B. Hamilton's 1951 work, which described patterns of male baldness and linked them to androgens. In 1975 dermatologist O'Tar Norwood revised the scheme after studying 1,000 patients, simplifying it to seven stages and adding the 'A' variants. 
Studies of androgenetic alopecia use the scale to define who is included and to describe severity, including trials of treatments and observational research on associated conditions.  In looksmaxxing forums it also acts as shared vocabulary for hairline status, from 'NW0' hairlines to 'baldmaxxing' at later stages.

name: Facial symmetry theory

chain: Left and right sides match more closely
angle.text: Looksmaxxers use symmetry as a guide for what to correct first, trying fillers, implants, posture work or bone-related methods to even out the face. Studies find a real but modest link between symmetry and attractiveness; changing asymmetry through posture or non-surgical methods is untested.

summary: The idea that more symmetrical faces are more attractive and signal good health; studies find a real but modest and context-dependent link, not a single decisive factor.
note: Studies disagree on strength, and some find symmetry raises attractiveness only when it also makes a face look typical.
currentQuick:
Facial symmetry theory holds that people find faces with matching left and right sides more attractive, partly because symmetry may signal health or developmental stability. Research since the 1990s, including work by Grammer and Thornhill (1994), reports that symmetrical faces tend to receive higher attractiveness ratings, independently of how average the face is. [1][2][3]
Looksmaxxing communities discuss symmetry heavily, from guides on correcting asymmetry to debates over whether it is the main driver of attractiveness. Researchers describe a more mixed picture: effects differ by sex of the face, rating method and whether the face looks typical. [1][4][5]
How it works: Proposed explanations include the 'good genes' or developmental-stability idea (symmetry as a visible sign of resistance to stress and disease), links between symmetry and perceived health, and that symmetry may simply make faces look more typical. Alternative explanations point to prenatal stress exposure rather than genetics. [1][6]
Risks and caveats: The theory carries no direct risk, but clinical literature notes that marked asymmetry from conditions such as facial palsy or craniofacial microsomia affects quality of life and may be treated surgically or with botulinum toxin. Community guides on correcting symmetry include procedures with their own medical risks. [7][8][9]
deepLead:
Facial symmetry theory is the proposal that bilateral symmetry of the face makes it more attractive and that this preference reflects an evolved sensitivity to cues of health and developmental stability. Researchers distinguish fluctuating asymmetry, random left-right differences, from directional asymmetry, a consistent bias across a population. 
A widely cited study by Grammer and Thornhill (1994) used computer-generated faces and reported that men and women preferred averageness and symmetry in opposite-sex faces.  Later work found that symmetry increases attractiveness ratings for both sexes, with stronger effects reported for female faces, and that symmetry and averageness contribute independently. 
Evidence for the health side of the theory is more mixed. Studies report that more symmetrical faces are rated as healthier, but links to objective health measures are described as inconsistent, and some researchers argue symmetry matters mainly through making a face look normal.  On looksmax.org symmetry is a staple topic, with guides on improving it and threads arguing about its importance.

name: Dimorphism theory

angle.text: Forum users treat masculine features such as a strong jaw and defined cheekbones as central to male attractiveness, and use the idea to choose beards, fat loss or procedures. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness is real but mixed.

summary: The idea that more sex-typical (masculine or feminine) facial features raise attractiveness; research on it is real but mixed.
note: Studies disagree on whether masculine male faces are rated as more attractive, and preferences vary by culture and context.
currentQuick:
Dimorphism theory is the looksmaxxing framing that faces differ between the sexes in measurable ways, and that more strongly sex-typical features (a pronounced jaw and brow in men, softer and more youthful features in women) are more attractive. Communities use it to explain why certain faces are rated highly.
Research on facial sexual dimorphism does exist, but its findings on attractiveness are mixed and depend on the population, culture, and what other traits are controlled for.
How it works: Proponents point to hormones, especially testosterone during puberty, shaping facial bone and soft tissue, and argue that observers read these features as signals of health or genetic quality. Researchers have proposed similar signalling hypotheses, while noting that the supporting evidence is inconsistent.
Risks and caveats: The theory itself is a descriptive framework with no direct risk. Applications that community members discuss, such as hormone use or surgery to change facial structure, carry their own medical risks that are covered in separate entries.
deepLead:
Dimorphism theory, in looksmaxxing usage, is the idea that facial and bodily differences between the sexes (sexual dimorphism) are central to perceived attractiveness, so that more strongly masculine male features and more strongly feminine female features are rated as better looking. It is a community framework rather than a single formal scientific theory, and it overlaps with academic work on facial masculinity and femininity.
Sexual dimorphism in humans is well documented in general terms: average differences in height, body mass, bone density, strength and hormone levels between adult males and females are described in the biological literature . Whether and when those differences make a face more attractive is less settled. Reviews of facial attractiveness research report that preferences for masculine male faces shift with factors such as a woman's menstrual-cycle phase, hormonal contraception use, self-rated attractiveness, relationship status and country . Some studies have found little link between facial masculinity and male attractiveness once perceived health is accounted for .

name: Ascension

angle.text: Ascension is the community word for a big improvement in looks over time, and forum threads document plans and progress with before-and-after photos. It names an outcome rather than a method, and results shown are individual self-reports.

summary: Community term for a large improvement in one's looks over time; the word describes an outcome, not a specific method.
note: Methods members associate with ascension vary widely and include some with documented medical risks, covered in their own entries.
currentQuick:
In looksmaxxing slang, ascension means a marked rise in perceived attractiveness, often shown through before-and-after photos. Members post ascension plans, protocols and progress updates on looksmax.org.
The term is a label for an outcome, so there is no single treatment or study behind it. What people do in pursuit of it ranges from grooming and fitness to medical interventions.
How it works: There is no single mechanism. Members describe combining changes such as body-fat loss, skin, hair, dental or surgical work, and in some cases hormones, depending on the plan.
Risks and caveats: Risks depend entirely on the methods used. Some forum posts describe emotional outcomes: one thread title holds that ascension will not cure psychological issues.
deepLead:
Ascension is looksmaxxing community slang for a substantial improvement in a person's looks, and the verb ascend is used for someone undertaking one. Looksmax.org has many threads titled with the word, including plans, protocols with promised before-and-after photos, and long progress updates .
The term is not a procedure, product or theory. Posts show members using it for outcomes reached through body-fat loss, among other routes, and for emotional reactions to looking better; one poster describes crying from joy after losing weight and no longer feeling subhuman, a framing other members questioned . A thread titled to the effect that ascension will not cure psychological issues shows the community also debates its limits .

name: Hairstyle maxxing

angle.text: Users pick a cut and styling to suit face shape, forehead size and hair type, and the change is visible as soon as the haircut is done. Research shows hair shapes first impressions, though how much it adds beyond the underlying face is debated.

summary: Choosing a cut and style to suit your face shape and hair type; cheap and reversible, with research showing hair shapes first impressions.
note: Tight or heavily traction-based styles are associated with traction alopecia in dermatology studies.
currentQuick:
Hairstyle maxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of picking a haircut and styling approach that suits the face, head shape and hair type. Forum members commonly argue that hair adds volume and texture to the face and can frame features, with some calling this a hair halo.
Research in person perception treats hairstyle, clothing and makeup as part of first impressions, though no trial has tested face-shape-matching rules as such.
How it works: Cut length, volume, fringe and parting change the visible outline of the head and how much forehead and eye area shows. Practitioners also consider hair type and growth pattern, and may use styling products or chemical straightening or waving.
Risks and caveats: Haircuts are reversible. Dermatology reviews report that tight, tension-heavy styles can cause traction alopecia, and chemical straightening or waving carries its own review literature.
deepLead:
Hairstyle maxxing refers to selecting hair length, cut and styling to improve overall appearance, particularly by matching style to face shape, forehead size and hair type. In forums the topic appears constantly as requests for hairstyle suggestions with photo posts, and members debate how much hair can compensate for other features .
A hairstyle is any arrangement of hair, and historically styles have signalled age, status, religion and identity . Choices are commonly described as depending on natural hair type and growth pattern, face and head shape, and personal and cultural factors . A 2023 review argues that dress, including hairstyle, makeup and accessories, influences first impressions and belongs in models of person perception .
